summary: Extends IPv6 multicast addressing so interface identifiers can be used to allocate multicast addresses. Each node can automatically build unique link-scoped multicast addresses from its link-local address without conflicts. It updates RFC 3306. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Each computer makes its own group-chat name from its unique name tag, so no two get the same name and nobody has to hand them out.

subtitle: How a node can build its own link-local IPv6 multicast addresses from its interface identifier, with no allocation server.

tldr.problem: IPv6 has no built-in way to hand out multicast addresses dynamically, and the unicast-prefix-based method of RFC 3306 needs allocation machinery that serverless networks such as ad-hoc and mobile networks do not have.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC puts the node's 64-bit interface identifier (IID), taken from its link-local unicast address after Duplicate Address Detection, in the multicast address. Because each IID is unique on the link, the node can create its own multicast addresses without conflicts.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3306 and applies only to link-scoped multicast addresses. Its uniqueness depends on Duplicate Address Detection, which can fail when networks merge.

today: RFC 4489 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2006. It updates RFC 3306 and has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC, according to the metadata for this entry.

sections.title: Why Generate Multicast Addresses from IIDs
sections.content:
RFC 4489 extends the multicast part of the IPv6 addressing architecture. The current architecture has no built-in support for dynamic address allocation. The extension lets a node use its Interface Identifier (IID) to allocate multicast addresses.

When a link-local unicast address is configured on an interface, the IID is uniquely determined. The node can then generate its own multicast addresses automatically and without conflicts, safely at any time after Duplicate Address Detection (DAD) has completed.

The RFC prefers this method over unicast-prefix-based multicast addresses (RFC 3306) for link-local scope, because no allocation server is needed. It says the method works better in serverless environments such as ad-hoc networks and network mobility. It restricts the use of the scop, plen and network prefix fields defined in RFC 3306.
sections.eli5: Normally someone has to hand out names for group chats. Here, each computer uses its own one-of-a-kind name tag to invent its group names, so nobody has to hand anything out.

sections.title: Where the Method Applies
sections.content:
The technique is meant for any environment where link-local scope IPv6 multicast addresses are assigned or selected. The RFC says it suits nodes that provide multicast services in a zeroconf or serverless environment. Such nodes generate their own multicast addresses, and hosts that use those services build the servers' addresses using Neighbor Discovery address resolution and well-known group IDs.

The scope limit is firm: the technique MUST only be used for link-scoped multicast addresses. For anything wider than link-local scope, use the methods in RFC 3306.
sections.eli5: This trick only works for chats among neighbours on the same street. For bigger groups across town you need the older method.

sections.title: The Link-Scoped Multicast Address Format
sections.content:
The new format replaces the 64-bit prefix field of RFC 3306 with the IID. From left to right the fields are: 11111111 (8 bits), flgs (4), scop (4), reserved (8), plen (8), IID (64) and group ID (32).

Four rules mark an address as this kind of multicast address: flgs MUST be 0011; scop MUST be less than or equal to 2; the reserved field MUST be zero; and plen is the special value 1111 1111 (decimal 255).

The IID MUST come only from the IID of the link-local unicast address on the interface, after DAD has completed. So the multicast address MUST NOT be created until DAD is done as part of auto-configuration. The group ID names a multicast application and only has to be unique within the host. It may also be set following the guidelines of RFC 3307.
sections.eli5: The address is like a label with a fixed start that says it is a group address, then the computer's own name tag, then a number for the particular chat. The computer may only write the label after it has checked that its name tag is not taken.

sections.title: A Worked Example
sections.content: In an Ethernet environment, suppose the link-local unicast address is FE80::A12:34FF:FE56:7890. The link-scoped multicast prefix of that node is then FF32:00FF:A12:34FF:FE56:7890::/96. The node's IID appears in the middle of the address, and the remaining 32 bits are free for group IDs.
sections.eli5: If a computer's name tag is a long string of numbers, its group chat names all begin with that same string, and only the last part changes from chat to chat.

sections.title: Lifetime of the Addresses
sections.content:
Link-scoped multicast addresses generally have no lifetime, because link-local unicast addresses have none either. In a mobile environment this is not quite true. The useful lifetime of such a multicast address is tied to the period during which the IID is known to be unique.

A conflict is possible if a new node in a merged network uses the same IID as a node that is already powered on. DAD also fails to guarantee uniqueness of the unicast address in that case, and the RFC says it does not try to address the issue.
sections.eli5: The names stay good as long as nobody else has the same name tag. If two groups of kids meet and two of them have the same tag, there can be a mix-up, and this document does not fix that.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Uniqueness of the multicast addresses is guaranteed by the DAD process, so a secure DAD process is needed for the method to be stable. The RFC proposes the mechanism in RFC 3041 for this purpose.

RFC 3041 describes privacy extensions for IPv6 stateless address autoconfiguration, used to form the IID of non-link-local unicast addresses. It cannot be used to make a link-local unicast address, so it cannot create the IID for a link-scoped multicast address. The RFC reasons that since RFC 3041 does not protect the privacy of link-local unicast addresses, protecting the privacy of IID-based link-local multicast addresses does not seem to be required.
sections.eli5: The whole scheme depends on every name tag really being unique, so the check that makes sure of that has to be trustworthy. Hiding the tags is not seen as important here.

fields.desc: Fixed leading bits that mark a multicast address.

fields.name: scop
fields.desc: MUST be less than or equal to 2.

fields.name: IID
fields.desc: Interface identifier of the link-local unicast address, taken after DAD completes.

fields.name: group ID
fields.desc: Identifies a multicast application; unique only within the host.
